articles.title: Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
articles.summary: The eight-year-old was in an enclosure with other children and a staff member when she was attacked.
body: The park keeps Arctic wolves, like those pictured, and grey wolves (file image)
An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.
She was inside an enclosure at the Johannismühle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.
They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".
The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.
The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.
The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.
The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.
It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.
Johannismühle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.
The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.
A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

articles.title: Ethiopia acquires Russian fighter jets and air defence systems amid war in Tigray
articles.summary: The acquisition of the warplanes comes amid ongoing fighting in northern Tigray region that started last month.
body: The acquisition of fighter jets comes amid ongoing tensions with Eritrea
Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity.

He said Ethiopia and Russia agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow.
The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.

Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in sub‑Saharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology."
"If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said.
Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military.
Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Su‑35 jets and S‑400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country.
The Su‑35, he noted, is equipped for both air‑to‑air and air‑to‑ground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200 kilometers.

Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts".
According to him, the jets are highly maneuverable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning.

When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority," Qalaab said.
Abiy said besides the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence.
Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts.
"We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said.

The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies.
Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty.
Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea.

articles.title: 'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
articles.summary: A micro-drama will use AI-assisted technology to edit old episodes of the Australian TV soap to focus on Margot Robbie's character.
body: Watch: Margot Robbie Neighbours episodes re-formatted into new social media series
Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.

Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.
Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.

Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.
Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.

In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".
The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.

"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".

The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.
Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.
"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.

Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.
That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.
Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.
"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.
"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."
Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.
Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".
"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".

Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".
The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.
The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.

It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.
"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

articles.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
articles.summary: Sanrio has apologised after its merchandise line with Japanese TV series Vivant drew criticism.
body: Sanrio says it will strengthen review processes for future collaborations
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".

"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".

Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."

When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".
Hello Kitty has been criticised on Chinese state media and Chinese social media
Hello Kitty is not the only internationally beloved figure to have faced such wrath in China in recent days.
Earlier this week, several Chinese brands dropped French footballer Kylian Mbappé over comments he had made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong - which he has since apologised for.
Vivant is about a Japanese salaryman who finds himself entangled in an international web of crime and espionage.

Its first season, which aired in 2023, was set in a fictional Central Asian country. Its second season, which premiered in July, features Chinese agents torturing a Japanese spy by cutting his fingers and stabbing his abdomen.
Chinese state outlets, including CCTV, argued that these tactics "highly overlap" with those historically used by Japanese troops against the Chinese, and that the drama "distorts the truth".
Masamine Ryuho, the president of Vivant's TV network TBS, said on Wednesday that the show was completely fictional and had no intentions of "disparaging any particular country".

articles.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
articles.summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey suspended its voyage and is working with passengers on "temporary living arrangements".
body: The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into its voyage around the world when it came to a stop in Cambodia
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.
The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.

Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.
Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day.

The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out.

"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed."
"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened."

Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.
"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia.
"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."
Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport.
Cruise passenger Holly Hennessey and her cat, Captain, have now found themselves in Cambodia
During their time onboard the Villa Vie Odyssey, passengers had access to several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month.
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea.
In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package.
Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election".
For Canen and Bodin the experience was "worth it", despite the fact it was shorter than expected.
"We loved our two years on Odyssey—the adventures, the places we visited and the friends we made along the way."
Many of the passengers have already made plans to "settle together off the ship, so those friendships and that sense of community are continuing on land", they said.
The couple plans to spend a few days in Sihanoukville, before travelling to different parts of South East Asia while they "figure out our next chapter".
But others, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Odyssey will set sail again soon.
"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said.
"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out."

articles.title: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
articles.summary: Authorities say the attacker in Belgrade was an underage male who was being monitored by security services.
body: Officers were visible outside the embassy in Belgrade later on Wednesday
Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".

The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.
Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".
Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.

Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level – meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.
The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.
Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.
Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.
This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.
The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.
Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

articles.title: Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
articles.summary: The energy minister described it as a "major milestone" for the East African nation.
body: The energy minister described it as a "major milestone" for the East African nation
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.

Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.
He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.
The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.
Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.
Gas from the field will be for domestic and industrial power generation and also for vehicles

"The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.
Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.
In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.
Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.
Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.

The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.

articles.title: Kenyan family protest extradition hearing delay of ex-British soldier accused of murdering kin
articles.summary: No official reason has been given for postponing next month’s hearing to May 2027, family says.
body: Agnes Wanjiru was discovered in a septic tank near a British army camp in Kenya in 2012
The family of a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by a British soldier 14 years ago has expressed outrage after an extradition hearing for the accused was postponed until May 2027.

Relatives of Agnes Wanjiru, whose body was found in a septic tank near a British army training camp in Kenya in 2012, described the delay as "completely unacceptable" and accused authorities of failing to keep them informed.

The hearing for Robert James Purkiss, a former British soldier accused of killing the 21-year-old mother, had been due next month. The family said it had now been postponed until May 2027. Purkiss was arrested in the UK last November and is fighting extradition to Kenya to face trial for murder. He denies the allegation.
Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.
"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.

"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."
The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.
It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.
The family said a UK court is expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.
Wanjiru disappeared in March 2012 after spending an evening at a hotel in Nanyuki, about 200km (124 miles) north of Nairobi, where British soldiers were stationed for training.
Her body was found nearly three months later in a septic tank at the hotel. She had suffered stab wounds to her chest and abdomen and left behind a five-month-old daughter.
A Kenyan inquest concluded in 2019 that she had been unlawfully killed by one or two British soldiers.
In September 2025, a Kenyan High Court issued an arrest warrant for a British national after prosecutors presented evidence they said justified bringing murder charges.
Purkiss' lawyers said he intended to contest extradition to Kenya.
The 38-year-old former soldier appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in February via video link, where he was further remanded in custody.
Last year, the then British Defence Secretary John Healey met Wanjiru's family during a visit to Kenya and pledged his government's support for efforts to secure justice.
The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

articles.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
articles.summary: The truce was originally planned for the stranded residents of Oleshky, and Russia and Ukraine say no breaches have been reported.
body: The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or water
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.

Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".

A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.

Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.

One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.

Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".
These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year

The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.

Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".

Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.

Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped
It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.

Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.
Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.

One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.

Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.
"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv.

articles.title: Europe's youth take to the streets - they feel locked out of a promising future
articles.summary: The last month has seen youth-driven demonstrations across Europe. What connects them?
body: Europe's youth take to the streets - they feel locked out of a promising future

From Milan, to Marseille, to Madrid and in so many other cities across Europe, streets have erupted in colourful, passionate protests in recent weeks. While most started peacefully, a large number ended in shocking scenes of violence and looting. There have been allegations of radical left-wing groups sparking riots intentionally and reports of police heavy-handedness.

We've seen thousands rallying in Rome and Florence. Hundreds of thousands across France. In Madrid, an encampment of tents has occupied a city-centre square since late September. In Lisbon, tens of thousands of mostly young people marched earlier this month. Tear gas and water cannon were used on protesters in Brussels, after young men dressed in black, their faces covered to hide their identities, threw rocks and firecrackers at police. In Albania, demonstrators alleging government corruption are demanding that their Prime Minister Edi Rama - already 13 years in power - stand down.
This continent feels volatile, socially and politically.

I've spent years in Europe reporting from a multitude of demonstrations, both peaceful and violent. I remember well the ardent Catalan pro-independence marches of 2017, the desperation and Molotov cocktails flying through Athens' streets during the 2015 Greek debt crisis, and various outbreaks of violence in France during President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office, sparked by fuel tax and pension reform proposals.
Hundreds of thousands have joined protests in France, some of which turned violent

But this feels different. Protests are exploding simultaneously across Europe and the majority of demonstrators - both peaceful and violent - are young. Some really young. Among those arrested, there's an eyebrow-raising number of minors. Over half of those detained in Barcelona scuffles last weekend were under 18. Minors were among those apprehended by police in Milan after clashes, according to Italy's LaPresse news agency.

Europe's governments, for the most part, have been careful to distinguish between looters and rioters on the one hand, and loud but peaceful, legally organised demonstrations on the other. The latter tend to focus around a particular cause. In the current protest wave, placards and chants mainly take aim at education grievances, social inequalities and the rising cost of living - though each country also comes with its own unique set of complaints.

What has triggered this public fury in Europe's youth, seemingly so quickly? Are all these demonstrations in some way interwoven? And with major European elections on the horizon, how will governments choose to respond - listening to protesters' concerns, or playing the law and order card to win support from older voters?
Students have taken to the streets in France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania - a more than 1,000-mile span of the continent.
Demonstrations are often organised in an ad hoc way via TikTok or Instagram. Belgium's interior minister has complained about what he calls the "TikTokisation" of protests.

Student unions play a role in organising marches, but they are also inspired by the actions of peers in other countries, even other continents. Think of the so-called Cockroach student movement in India - a Gen Z social and political protest movement that emerged in May this year, starting with criticism of the Indian education system.

France, where the current wave of student protests kicked off in late September, fuelled by student complaints over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, is a stand-out catalyst in Europe. There's a saying in neighbouring Belgium: whenever it pours in Paris, it at least drizzles in Brussels. The Belgian capital and the town of Liège have also now seen weeks of protesting youngsters.
In Athens, school pupils and teachers have demonstrated over education and the cost of living
In Barcelona this weekend, students were encouraged to demonstrate under the social media hashtag #InstitutsIndignats, echoing the French slogan, Lycées Indignés (Outraged High Schools).

In Athens, 17-year-old Greek school pupil Yiannis Papanikolaou told AFP: "School buildings are terrible and poorly maintained… I think something might change, because of what France is doing, France will spur Greece."

There's a continent-wide sense of economic malaise felt by large numbers of young people – and it goes far beyond education. They worry about the environment, and fret that AI will rob them of job opportunities. They fear the spiralling cost of living could prevent them from finishing their education and stop them buying or renting a home big enough to start a family.

In Madrid and in Lisbon, frustration has focused on the prohibitive price tag attached to housing. Portuguese Instagram-linked campaigns stated "enough is enough" and called on people to take to the streets as peers had done in Spain.

In Lisbon, Carolina ⁠Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher, said she faces losing her home as her rental contract nears expiry. "I'm the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I've done, I still can't make it," she told Reuters.

It's an anger shared by 22-year-old Riccardo, a protester in Italy's financial capital, Milan. "Even if we don't manage to throw the country into chaos like in France or block every road like in Spain, the aim is at least people will start talking about these issues again," he told AFP.

And it's certainly not just young people on the left of politics who are angry. At the presidential campaign launch of French nationalist Marine Le Pen last weekend, young supporters described different concerns to me. Calling themselves the "silent majority" - not (yet) out demonstrating - they say they also worry deeply about "uncontrolled immigration" and safety on France's streets, as well as the cost of living.

The outpouring of discontent has spread beyond young people to include trade unions, France's disparate Yellow Jacket movement that protested against the cost of living crisis during Macron's first term, and other citizens' initiatives. This weekend, Kent in coastal southern England saw two protests, one for and one against immigration.
This miscellaneous mix of protests can seem confusing.

Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, speaks of a build-up of cascading, competing crises in Europe, none of which have ever been properly resolved, he says. That sense of pent-up anger is now bubbling over onto the streets.
Anti-government marches have swept through Tirana, the Albanian capital

"One crisis layers on top of the other," he told me. "The financial crisis of 2007-8, the migrant crisis of 2015, the environmental crisis, Covid, inflation after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and now again with the war in the Gulf."
Leonard says different "tribes" have emerged out of these crises. Social media consumption and algorithms harden their differing perspectives, leading to a real sense of polarisation in Europe.
"We've already seen this in the US," says Leonard. "A sense of 'my crisis is more important than your crisis'."

Nathalie Tocci, a former Italian government adviser who is now a politics professor at Johns Hopkins University, tells me we shouldn't be so taken aback by the protests, or the youth engagement in them.

"We tend to think of youngsters as politically switched off and disinterested. We think they don't bother to go out to vote etc, but they are truly engaged," she told me, "just in a different, more grassroots way. Think of the "Fridays for the Future [environmental movement] across Europe a few years ago, or the demonstrations against Israel's actions in Gaza after 7 October.

She points to the student-led protest movement in Serbia, which recently defeated long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić in parliamentary elections. "It's quite something. They kept going and going, for more than two years. What sticking power will these new European street demos have? That's not yet clear."
Belgian security services say there is "opportunistic" violence on the fringes of legally approved protests
And what about the looting and the violence?
Intelligence services in France and Belgium have described looting on the edges of legally approved protests as mainly opportunistic.

The rioting, they suggest, is a mixture of "mindless violence" - also identified by the Spanish authorities in Barcelona to describe clashes there at the weekend - plus mayhem intentionally orchestrated by youth from ultra-left radical groups.

Tocci reminded me that, in Italy, you can hear the word "maranza" being used by some Italians upset by the perpetrators of destruction seemingly for the sake of it: smashing or burning cars or public bins, for example.

In France, rioters are often described as "casseurs" - people who break things. But in private, some use a more politically charged term - "racaille". Like "maranza" in Italy, it's pejorative slang, generally used to describe disaffected, rowdy urban youths frequently from working-class and/or immigrant backgrounds. It was used in October 2005 by then-French Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, to describe young delinquents and rioters during a tense visit to the housing projects of Paris suburb Argenteuil.

French media has also asked whether there's been an alliance of convenience, however informal or incidental, between two groups of youths: ultra-left activists and young people from France's disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Like the anti-capitalist left, youth from public housing projects on the outskirts of French cities (known as the banlieues) often feel discriminated against, and complain of police heavy handedness towards them.
Puerta del Sol square in Madrid has been occupied by tents since late September

The political right and centre in France, including Macron, blame left-wing radical groups and "delinquents" for planning the riots. In contrast to Le Pen's National Rally Party, they have not mentioned a link with past or current immigration to France.

Critics accuse anti-immigration parties in Europe of trying to capitalise from the riots to score political points. In Belgium, the anti-immigration opposition Flemish nationalist party, Vlaams Belang, appeared to blame migrants for violence in Liège and Brussels, describing the riots as "imported" and blaming a failure of integration and of open borders. Belgium's Interior Minister Bernard Quentin has pointed the finger at ultra-left groups.
Fresh mass demonstrations have been planned over the next days in France and in Italy.
Governments are trying to crack down on the violence. There have been thousands of arrests, and Italy and France have promised to impose a "you break it, you pay for it" policy for rioters.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is also making parents of minors liable for damage caused by their kids, including deducting welfare support received by the family. The Civil Code in France already holds parents who live with their children liable for damage they cause.

But some of these European governments may not be in power for long. All the big EU countries have been holding, or will hold, key elections in the coming months. France's presidential vote is considered the most pivotal for Europe. Le Pen is consistently polling far ahead of her rivals. It's assumed the unrest on French streets is helping her, thanks to her party's law and order message.

In Spain, Italy, Germany and Poland, nationalist, tough-on-immigration parties are also polling well. These parties promise to restore order and national pride. Leonard believes populist or non-traditional parties on the left and the right have become "crisis entrepreneurs", using the turbulent situation in Europe to attract disaffected voters.
Meanwhile, Europe's political mainstream faces a crisis of leadership, says Grégoire Roos, director of Europe at the Chatham House think tank.
I would argue they also face a crisis of legitimacy. The fact that so many people - the young and not so young - are out protesting indicates they have failed to get on top of things.
Europe's car makers are in crisis. Will the threat of war rescue them?
Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
How population decline is exposing Germany's old divides

But it's not at all clear that new elections will resolve public frustration. France is so polarised, for example, that if Le Pen were to become president, many predict her opponents would fill French streets in anger.

Modern Europe is built on an assumption that citizens pay taxes and obey laws. In exchange, they get good public services, like education and healthcare, personal safety and a stable society that follows certain rules and regulations.
But this "social contract" has clearly eroded, says Roos.
Looking at the ferment on Europe's streets, this moment of protest looks likely to continue.

articles.title: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
articles.summary: Properties where someone has died in tragic circumstances can have big reductions in price.
body: The previous occupant of Ryua's apartment, pictured here, sadly took their own life
From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.
"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.
"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."
While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.
"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.
Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.
Ryua says that she shares her Tokyo apartment with a ghost

Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.

These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.

For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.
Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.
For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.

By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.

Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.

While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.

"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."
The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.
But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

The 79-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her – there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.
Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.
"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."
Diane Tincher says she got a 50% reduction on her home in rural Japan

Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.
It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.
Diane Tincher got a huge discount on her home in rural Japan
Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.

Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap., external
Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

articles.title: How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios
articles.summary: With 85% of votes counted, all signs point to an impasse. The most likely outcome may be new elections.
body: Neither Gadi Eisenkot (left) or Benjamin Netanyahu (right) are projected to win enough seats for a majority
Israel looks to be in political deadlock.
With 85% of votes counted after Tuesday's election, neither the incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, nor the bloc of his key challenger Gadi Eisenkot look set to win a majority.
In order to form a government, it looks likely one of the leading parties would have to break their campaign promises - meaning the most probable outcome may well be new elections.
Here are four possible scenarios.
Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?
Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.

Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".
But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.

Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government" - remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.

One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.
This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.
This would be a seismic shift for Israeli politics. Only one independent Arab party has ever formally been part of a coalition, in 2021, and it didn't last long.
Eisenkot and every other Jewish party in his bloc bar one have already ruled out entering government with them. But right now, it's the opposition's only path to a majority.

The Arab parties were the story of election night. They look to have defied expectations and could gain a record 19 seats - helped by an unprecedented turnout from Israel's Arab population, who account for about one-fifth of the country and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout last night was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history.

The United Arab list, who are currently projected to win around 7 seats, have said they'd join an opposition government, while The Joint List, who are projected to win 12 seats, have said they'd support one from outside.

However, the only Jewish leader advocating this scenario right now is The Democrats' Yair Golan. And a coalition like this would be very fragile, especially on issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The fact there is such a unified front from the otherwise fragmented Jewish parties against Arab participation points to Israel's deep divisions.
Could Netanyahu persuade the right-wing parties in Eisenkot's bloc to break away and join his coalition?

The two most likely candidates for this are Naftali Bennett - joint-leader of the Beyachad political alliance - and Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party. They are both right-wingers who are hardline on security, and share some political ground with Netanyahu.

But both campaigned explicitly to oust him, and to extend military conscription to the ultra-Orthodox - bringing them into direct conflict with the two ultra-Orthodox parties already part of Netanyahu's government. So it's difficult to see them joining forces.
Some have suggested Bennett and Lieberman's parties could replace the ultra-Orthodox parties, but current electoral math suggests that grouping may not have the seats needed for a majority.
If none of the above scenarios can be negotiated, the default outcome would be new elections.
Many would see this as a tacit win for Netanyahu, who would remain as caretaker PM until the new elections take place - and he may believe he has a better chance of winning them.

Some analysts think the high Arab turnout would not be repeated - especially if their record representation in parliament led to no change. And it could also mobilise more right-wing voters in a second poll.
Netanyahu may also bet that the estimated 70,000 Israelis who flew home from abroad to vote, and are thought to skew against him, wouldn't do so again.
Additionally, several right-wing parties who failed to pass the electoral threshold of 3.25% may attract fewer votes or may not even run, thereby bringing more votes to Likud and its allies.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title: What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
articles.summary: More than 500 passengers were on board the trains when the incident occurred in the province of Toledo, south of Madrid.
body: Watch: Aerial footage shows train crash scene
Two trains have collided in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.
Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe train and another of the Iryo company, which covers the Madrid to Seville route.
So far at least 30 people are confirmed to have died in the incident with casualty numbers expected to rise.
Here is what we know about the crash so far.
The two trains collided just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.

The accident happened when a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to the south of the country collided with another train that was apparently stationary. The crash caused at least two carriages to fall down an embankment.
Broadcaster RTVE, quoting the transport ministry, said a Renfe train rear-ended an Iryo train.
Renfe is Spain's national state-owned railway company while Iryo is a private high-speed railway operator.
All train traffic on this line has been stopped at stations along the route, Adif said.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia remain suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
Aerial footage shows the extent of the damage and the emergency response
The cause has not been confirmed, though reports in Spain suggest a high-speed train hit another train which had stopped on the tracks.
More than 500 people were believed to be on board both trains.

Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
A former government minister was also among those reported missing.
The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, Fátima Báñez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.
Local leader Emiliano García-Page, president of Castilla-La Mancha, said "at least 30" people are now confirmed to have died.
Speaking separately to Spanish media, he warned the death toll could increase further.
Eighty people are being treated for injuries, according to authorities, with 50 of the casualties said to be in a serious condition.
A huge emergency response is underway
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo".

"I remain in constant contact with the Minister of Transport, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha," Sánchez said on X, adding that emergency services were working on the ground "to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations".
"My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."
Sánchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Spanish news agency have reported that hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash.

A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

articles.title: Spain begins mourning period after train crash as search continues for victims in wreckage
articles.summary: Emergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples
body: Spain has begun three days of mourning to commemorate the 68 people who died in a high-speed rail collision as hospitals continue to treat scores of injured passengers and rescuers scour the wreckage of the two trains for victims.

The trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo – were heading from Madrid on Wednesday to the southern region of Andalucía on the same line when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.

The deadly crash came 10 months after 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s large, modern high-speed rail network after the transport minister, Óscar Puente, said rear-end collisions such as Wednesday’s were “highly unlikely”, and suggested the accident could have been caused by human error under “inexplicable” circumstances.

He said the LZB signalling system, which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied, had gone down at about 8.30am local time due to a computer malfunction. As a result, an estimated six trains had been halted along a stretch of about 63km of track, Puente added.

The task of monitoring the rail lines then fell to a 24-hour command centre in Madrid. Minutes after the computer malfunction, the centre instructed at least two of the trains to continue as normal, despite the fact that there was still a “stop signal” in place, the minister added.

“It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”

Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight to find further victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes. At daybreak, police once again launched drones to survey the crash site.

“Rescue teams are still working very carefully, because we still can’t say with certainty that ​there are no more victims trapped in the twisted wreckage,” ‌Esther Padilla, a spokesperson for the ‌regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told TVE.
“A canine unit was deployed yesterday. They will go back in today to make sure ‌that nobody else remains there.”

Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on Wednesday that more victims were likely to be found as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.

Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety after what was Europe’s deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain that killed 80 people.
Related: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain

The Guardia Civil police force has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid. The force said 64 people had been reported missing by relatives by Thursday morning.

A school in Urda, which lies around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been turned into an information centre where relatives can enquire about their loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who had arrived, some of them in tears.

Carmen García, a Red Cross psychologist, said “long and hard hours” lay ahead and that “every person will manage it in their own way”. She added: “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated.”
José Miguel Fernández, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families.

“It is important for relatives to find their loved ones, even if they have died, because the grieving process is quicker when you have been able to say goodbye at that final moment,” he told Onda Cero radio.
Speaking in Urda on Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.

The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.
Related: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
Survivors have spoken of being thrown from their seats by the impact of the crash, and of trying to help the injured in the immediate aftermath.
The first victim to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil officer, José Manuel Chacón.

The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the conservative People’s party (PP) and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.

The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry
articles.summary: Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’
body: The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.

Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.
In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.
Related: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey

The backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit of Japan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.
Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.

The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.
In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.

Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.
“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”
The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.

Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off a diplomatic row in November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.
Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.
China is a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.
The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.

The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé was dropped by several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred to Mao Zedong as a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Everything you need to know about Burnham’s first budget
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: There’s help on household energy bills and a modest bank tax, but big questions about this government’s long term vision remain unanswered
body: Good morning. As chancellor John Healey delivered the first budget of the Burnham government yesterday afternoon, the now-familiar phrasings were all in there: “breathing space” for households, “growth in every postcode,” and setting the foundations for a “radical rewiring of the state.”
But political ambition met economic reality, as the chancellor hammered home the scale of damage inflicted on the public finances by the war in the Middle East.

Just over 100 days into Andy Burnham’s premiership, this was not the all-guns-blazing transformative change of a government that styled itself as the most radical since Margaret Thatcher, but a confetti of micro-measures in a budget so quiet it at times barely whispered. Which is just what the City ordered, rewarding Burnham and Healey with a day of falling bond yields. But was this really the first step in kicking 40 years of neoliberalism into touch?

This morning I’ll take you through the key takeaways, and address the one question nobody else dares to: if this budget was a New Order track, would it be more Regret than True Faith? But first, the headlines.

Spain | Spain has begun three days of mourning after a high-speed rail collision – its second this year – killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
US midterms | Barack Obama, speaking at a campaign rally in suburban Atlanta, offered a closing argument for Democrats in the final week of the midterm election campaign.
UK news | Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of harassing two journalists to the point it caused them fear of violence.

Israel | Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.

Media | Two news organisations have a duty to the public and their sources to publish allegations of exploitative sexual behaviour by a well-known figure despite claims he is “highly likely” to attempt suicide, the high court has heard.

Compare John Healey’s comms with the pre-budget media blitz of previous chancellor Rachel Reeves (which resulted in a gripping row about productivity forecasts, requiring everyone to pretend they understood what fiscal headroom was). The run-up to this year’s budget was – to the entertaining chagrin of some Westminster commentators – leak-free, with the precision-controlled release of ‘everyday fixes’, such as removing tariffs from 100 food items, from baked beans to boiled sweets – a move promptly dismissed as gherkinomics by the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith.

But was this controlled media strategy simply because there wasn’t… that much to leak? To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, Healey leaned into incremental change, rather than radical transformation, as he warned the Commons that the country was facing not light fiscal headwinds but “global economic storms”.

Indeed, after Healey finished speaking, the government’s independent forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, issued a sharp downgrade to its growth forecast for 2027, warning British households face a “pretty grim picture” for living standards as Trump’s open-ended war on Iran triggers a fresh cost of living crisis. He nonetheless promised a series of fixes to help with the cost of living, including the one measure that could plausibly be described as the proverbial hat-exiting rabbit, a new £100 energy payment for millions of households. But more difficult decisions were delayed until next year’s spending review.

In his 56-minute speech, Healey’s major announcements included plans to: * Give 20m households in council tax bands A to D in England a £100 household energy payment this winter, with equivalent funding for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (immediately after the announcement, Andrew Sparrow over on our politics live blog discovered that gov.uk’s council tax band checker had glitched under the strain.)
* Extend the VAT cut on electricity until July 2027, which Healey says will take £50 off the annual price cap.

* Abolish standing charges, a fixed daily fee on top of usage, on gas bills – this should save two-thirds of us an average of £45 a year, and is likely to help poorer households, which use less gas, so the standing charge makes up a bigger proportion of their bill.
* Extend the 5p fuel duty cut to July 2027.
* Introduce a new Pension Tax Allowance for lower income pensioners that means they won’t be taxed on any of their state pension.
* Abolish the controversial cliff-edge rule for carers’ allowance, a scandal exposed by the Guardian last year that has plunged hundreds of thousands of unpaid carers into life-changing debt.
* Ditch plans to slash the annual cash Isa allowance, overturning the decision by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to cut the amount you can save in tax-free accounts from £20,000 to £12,000 a year.
* Help for the high street: small business rate relief raised from £12,000 to £18,000

* Extra economic and military support for Ukraine worth £10bn based on loans and export finance guarantees, Healey said President Zelensky had told him “you’ve made my day” when he shared the details ahead of the budget speech.

Sticking with Labour’s pledge not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance, Healey raised the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for the next 15 months. He said this would pay for immediate support with energy bills, but campaigners and organisations like the TUC, which has been pushing for a much higher surcharge, will probably be disappointed he didn’t go further for longer. He said the support package would also be paid for by an unexpected two percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and non-Isa savers.

Healey also raised taxes on higher stakes gambling machines by 5% to 25%, and excluded adult games centres as well as vape shops from business rates relief. Other measures include a clampdown on online sellers like Amazon, eBay and Temu avoiding VAT on their platforms, and stronger compliance powers for HMRC to collect overdue tax.

* The National Minimum Wage is to rise by 3.9%, but Healey faces fierce criticism for not fulfilling the manifesto pledge to equalise the lower minimum wage paid to people under 21 with the rate for older workers.

* Healey rejected calls by senior Labour MPs to raise capital gains tax to the same levels as income tax after influential figures, including the former Treasury minister Jim O’Neill, warned it would harm incentives for “wealth creators”.
* The chancellor was reported to be considering lowering the threshold for Reeves’s mansion tax from £2m to £1.5m, but London MPs pushed back.

* Although government departments are facing real-term cuts, Healey made no mention of topping up their cash budgets. Paul Johnson, former director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, suggested the real story of the budget was Labour kicking the can down the road.
“We know who we are, we know where we’re going, we can see the Britain we want to be,” Healey concluded with a flourish, before sitting down for a big hug with Andy.

But did his budget bring British voters any closer to knowing what the Burnham government stands for? Responding to Healey’s speech, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said that most people listening would think “is that it?” And this question was being posed by critical friends of Labour too.

The chancellor was careful to acknowledge the staging posts to come – substantial reports from Alan Milburn and Stephen Timms, on Neets and Pip respectively, will be published next month and offer more detail on proposed changes to welfare spending. The spending review next spring will set out plans to meet Nato commitments on defence. But in the interim, did Healey offer enough? As Andrew Sparrow pointed out, perhaps sensitive to the charge that there is not much radicalism to see here, both Healey and Burnham are presenting the changes to gas standing charges as the start of an ambitious reform of “our broken energy market” – while accepting that “won’t happen overnight”. Government ministers talking up the budget in the evening media rounds also pointed to the section of the budget detailing Healey’s “roadmap for fiscal devolution” as further evidence of the vision thing.

Our early analysis suggests he is at least speaking people’s language.
