It was, as a Guardian editorial noted, “one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history”.

The students’ extraordinary feat came as Europe has been rocked by weeks of protests. From Porto to Paris and Madrid to Milan, analysts have pointed to the common thread that weaves through the diverse protests: a view that the social contract has broken down, leaving younger generations bracing for a future in which they will be worse off than their parents.

The election result in Serbia lays bare the power of these protests to reshape politics, postdoctoral researcher Aleksandar Matković noted this week. Could it be, as WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange once told an interviewer in Belgrade, that Serbia is “a country where the future happens first”?

Matković drew on his involvement inside the student movement to offer a singular window into all that had gone into their win, citing discussions that had stretched as long as six hours as the students laid the groundwork for their entry into politics. “The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics,” he wrote.

Their win sparked joy across Serbia, sending tens of thousands of jubilant revelers on to streets across the country. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” Sara, 24, told the Guardian.
Hours later supporters of the movement appeared again, this time to clean up after a night of raucous celebrations.

The movement now faces a tremendous task – particularly given that it has no hierarchy or leader. For more than a decade, Vučić’s party had transformed the state, tightening its grip on media, stuffing institutions with loyalists to the party and wielding ministries and Serbian institutions as political tools.

The movement won 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving a comfortable majority to a slate of candidates who range from academics to athletes, and who were chosen via student assemblies in the lead-up to the election. As one candidate told my colleagues on Monday, the top priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.

Underpinning the movement is an 11-point plan, which includes ridding the country of corruption, reforming the judiciary and media and improving access to healthcare. “We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory,” one member of the movement wrote in the Guardian this week. “Rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.”

And while their plans for power take shape, the impact of their bold experiment will certainly be felt far beyond Serbia. The country applied to join the European Union in 2009, but the process has largely stalled in recent years. Now, much like in neighbouring Hungary, the elections have ushered in the possibility of a fresh start along with hope of a democratic resurgence in central Europe.

As EU officials sent their congratulations this week to the students, whose policy platform promises to put the question of future EU membership to a referendum, a note of optimism laced their messages. “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, said on social media.
Marta Kos, the EU’s enlargement commissioner, was more direct. “A new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together,” she wrote on social media.

It was a stunning reversal of fortunes for the students who last year felt they had to cycle more than 1,300km (780 miles) to make their voices heard. Now – after nearly two years of protests that were met with detentions on trumped-up evidence, illegal surveillance, threats and job losses – it seems they might have a chance to fulfil their wish of bringing Europe to Serbia.

articles.title: Passengers stranded in Cambodia after cruise halted due to high fuel costs
articles.summary: The luxury MV Odyssey ship slated for a years-long voyage around the world suspends operations amid high fuel prices
body: A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was forced to suspend its operations and leave passengers stranded in Cambodia because of high fuel prices.

The ship, known as the MV Odyssey, had been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials told the Associated Press. The ship has a 650-passenger capacity.

The Florida-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey, the company that operates the cruise line, said it was working with passengers on organizing “temporary living arrangements”. The cruise ship had begun its journey in Belfast in October 2024 for what was described as a “continuous voyage around the world”.

“Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure,” a statement on the company’s website said. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalization alternatives over the next 60 days.”
The ship is now docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with a departure date still unclear.

The price of fuel across the world has jumped since the start of the US war on Iran earlier this year. The ship’s operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800.
The strait of Hormuz, which transports much of the world’s oil, has effectively been closed since 28 February, the beginning of the war. Oil prices climbed to above $117 a barrel this month.

One resident on the ship, Randy Cassingham, wrote in a blogpost that he only discovered the cruise route’s cancellation after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship on Monday morning.

“It of course didn’t come from out of the blue: we’ve been well aware of problems,” Cassingham wrote. “It was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the mentioned crisis in fuel cost and availability, and more.”

Pamela Reckamp, a 59-year-old resident of the ship, told NBC News that company officials on the ship had held a meeting last month where they asked cabin owners to help them raise $1m so the ship could depart Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.
“She said: ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp said. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”

Carol Larson, 69, lived on the ship for 18 months along with her sister, Crystal Lavering, 72, she told the Associated Press. Larson, who is from California, expressed hopes that the journey could still be salvaged because she said the decision to live at sea had improved her health.

Larson told the outlet that she bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, with additional monthly maintenance fees under a program that offered her the option of living onboard the ship for up to 15 years.

Larson blamed Donald Trump for the problems facing the ship and the suspended journey, as the war on Iran caused fuel costs to rise significantly. Despite the issues, however, Larson said she did not regret her investment.

“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk,” she said. “From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising.”

articles.title: Israel election: what we know so far
articles.summary: With nearly all votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but main opponents also fail to gain outright majority; marked gains by Palestinian parties
body: With almost all votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but his main opponents, an alliance of Jewish Israeli parties unofficially led by Gadi Eisenkot, have also failed to gain an outright majority.

Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 53 seats under the current vote share, but this could change further. The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 48 seats and the Palestinian parties on 19 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset.
The remainder of votes to be counted come from absentee ballots, according to Israeli media. We can expect absentee ballots to be counted on Wednesday night, with final results by Thursday.

The Palestinian Israeli parties have received a historically strong vote. The Joint List, a new ticket of several Arab-majority parties, triumphed with at least 12 seats, while Ra’am, the other Islamic party, won seven.

The key question is whether the Eisenkot-led “Change” bloc (consisting of the rightwinger Naftali Bennett’s Together party, the centre-left Yair Golan’s Democrats and the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party) will partner with Palestinian Israeli parties or if they will resort to a new election, or even working with Netanyahu.

Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters that official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”. He told his supporters that the country must “establish a strong, rightwing national government” – adding that a government that relied on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.

Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv that the “Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister … a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics”. In his speech, he also warned Netanyahu not to “use Israel’s security” for political ends, playing on fears that the prime minister could use this period of uncertainty to launch a new attack on Iran.

The Palestinian Israeli vote, which represents about 20% of the population, had long been seen as a decisive factor for who will be able to form government, and the high turnout of this election was driven by the community experiencing increased racism and discrimination under Netanyahu’s government.
This is the most voted-for election in Israel’s political history, with many Israelis flying back into the country to cast their vote, and nearly 80% of IDF soldiers voting.
Donald Trump said his endorsement had helped Netanyahu perform better than polling estimates.

articles.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
articles.summary: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website
body: Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Related: The news website that’s keeping press freedom alive in Egypt | Leslie T Chang
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

articles.title: Soviet troops invade Hungary – archive, 1956
articles.summary: On 4 November 1956, Russian forces moved into Budapest as part of an offensive against a national uprising that called for democratic reforms and an end to Soviet occupation
body: Before dawn yesterday Soviet armoured forces moved into Budapest and attacked “rebel” strongholds. At 8am the Soviet High Command in Hungary ordered Imre Nagy’s government to surrender by noon “or Budapest will be bombed”. Soviet armoured forces then went into action. Just after 1pm Moscow radio announced: “The Hungarian counter-revolution has been crushed.”

A mid-afternoon Moscow radio bulletin said that negligible groups of insurgents were offering resistance in Budapest but were being crushed. The radio also announced that a new “Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Government” had been formed under János Kádár, the former “Titoist” who became first secretary of the Communist party at one point in the rebellion.
Related: The Hungarian revolution begins – archive, October 1956

Budapest radio had gone off the air at 8.10am with a woman’s appeal to “help Hungary … help, help, help …” In mid-afternoon a Vienna monitor picked up what was apparently the last rebel-held radio station in Hungary. It broadcast repeated calls for help.

Civilised people of the world. On the watch tower of 1,000-year-old Hungary the last flames begin to go out. Soviet tanks and guns are roaring over Hungarian soil. Our women – mothers and daughters – are sitting in dread. They still have terrible memories of the army’s entry in 1945. Save our souls. This word may be the last from the last Hungarian freedom station. Listen to our call. Help us – not with advice, not with words, but with action, with soldiers and arms.

The last news from Budapest itself reached the British Foreign Office in mid-afternoon. This said that Soviet troops were in control of key points and bridges in the city, although gunfire was still in progress. Other reports said that Mr Nagy, who attempted to restore democracy in the country after the insurrection, was under arrest, together with members of his government.

Mr Nagy – now arrested – had given news of the Soviet attack to the world in a dramatic broadcast over Budapest radio. He spoke in English and then repeated his message in Hungarian. “This is Imre Nagy speaking,” he said. “In the early hours of this morning, Soviet troops started to attack the Hungarian capital with the apparent purpose of overthrowing the democratic government of the Hungarian People’s Republic.” After broadcasting frequent appeals to Russian troops not to fire on peaceful citizens, the radio then went off the air.

Eisenhower appeals to BulganinMr Nagy, before he disappeared, had appealed through the British Legation for immediate intervention by the United Nations. Russia vetoed discussion of Hungary in the Security Council but the General Assembly, where the veto does not rule, voted overwhelmingly for an American resolution calling on the Soviet Union to halt its armed attack on Hungary and withdraw all its forces “without delay.”

President Dwight D Eisenhower sent an urgent message to Marshal Bulganin, the Soviet Premier, asking him to withdraw the Soviet troops. The president expressed “shock and dismay” at the Soviet attack on the Hungarian people and urged that Hungary be given the right to choose its own government.

Sopron, 4 NovemberIn this small town, the most westerly in Hungary, the last minutes of the revolution ran out to the rattle of machine-gun fire, the rumble of Soviet tanks, the screams and tears of women, and the singing of the Hungarian national anthem.

Until 3pm, no Russian troops had entered Sopron, but they were known to be all around it, in the hills and woods. I arrived at Klingenbach, the nearest point in Austria, at three o’clock and decided to go in and have a look for myself. Approaching the Klingenbach I saw streams of Hungarian refugees, walking in little groups along the road, carrying their worldly belongings on their backs, or on oxcarts, handcarts or bicycles.Continue reading.
Related: Political turmoil and street protests: rebellion’s bitter legacy lives on

The “forest fire,” as the prime minister calls it, has not been put out. The flames are rising – and not only in the Middle East. They have spread to eastern Europe. For months or years to come it will be a matter of debate whether Britain’s attack on Egypt sparked Russia’s attack on Hungary. To say the least however, it is possible that British aggression tipped the scales in Soviet planning towards violent action: and British defiance of Assembly resolutions has sapped the strength of the United Nations at a most critical moment. Where Britain has rejected the Assembly’s wishes, Russia (though her crime may be greater) can follow. For the present, Hungary is doomed.

For Hungary and eastern Europe there is tragically little that can be done. Russia can be condemned in the United Nations, but after the past week’s events that will mean little. It remains to be seen whether Russia is turning back entirely to a Stalinist line in foreign policy. Certainly the bankruptcy of its ideology has been displayed to the world in Hungary. If brute force is to be its method in future, we must expect mounting tension also between east and west in Europe.This is an edited extract. Read in full.

Throughout the western countries governments and peoples yesterday protested against the Russians’ suppression of the Hungarian revolt. Even in Poland, still a communist country, a party leader expressed sympathy with the Hungarians.

The official Yugoslav reaction was equivocal. The official news agency, Tanjug, said the use of foreign troops to clear up the internal affairs of a nation was contrary to the principles of Yugoslavia’s foreign policy, “but we cannot avoid the fact that the use of those troops was the result of a negative development in Hungary. Yugoslavs have with great concern followed the strong tendencies of reactionary elements, especially in Budapest – with murders of innocent people, the setting fire to books, and slogans which were smelling of the return to the Horthy era.”

Moscow Radio accused Britain and France of raising the Hungarian question in the United Nations as a “smokescreen for the Anglo-French aggression in the Suez canal zone.” The broadcast went on: “Representatives of certain western powers should be the last ones to pose as defenders of the Hungarian people. It was precisely the long subversive activity of the imperialist powers that inspired and directed the actions of the reactionary forces in Budapest.”
Paris: The French foreign minister, M Pineau, said France regretted that the United Nations had preferred to talk about Egypt rather than support the valiant Hungarian people.

Berlin: The West Berlin radio stations played solemn music in contrast to their usually light Sunday programme. The communist radio of East Berlin continued its normal programme, including dance music. The East German Radio said it had received numerous telephone calls from workers offering help for Hungary or suggesting the creation of an “international brigade to assist the Hungarian workers in the struggle for freedom.”
Copenhagen: About a thousand Danish students demonstrated outside the Russian embassy.

articles.title: ‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program
articles.summary: As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, retired admiral Peter Briggs says personnel is one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces
body: Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned.

As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program.
Related: We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up?

As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its six diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete.
The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – more than double the number needed for the Collins class.
The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.

“Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said.
“By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.”
But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats.
“We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said.
“You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.”
About 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-Aukus submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK.
“The personnel side is a huge issue but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said.
Related: Hegseth calls US-built nuclear submarines the ‘apex predator’ of the seas. But are they right for Australia?
The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements.
The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track.
Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians.

After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program, which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet.
From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling.

Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.
Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated.
Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment.
The USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”.
Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons.

It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port.
The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.
Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties.
In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms.
Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”.
Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said.
“Being nuclear-powered is a massive advantage.”

articles.title: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit
articles.summary: Royal tour of Caribbean comes as poll suggests majority support among younger Britons for dialogue on slavery reparations
body: King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour.

The king arrived in the Bahamas on Tuesday to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.
His arrival comes as a poll suggested strong support among young people and Labour voters in the UK for a dialogue on slavery reparations.

The poll, conducted by More in Common last week and published by the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, found that 40% of Britons supported a meeting on reparatory justice, while 19% were undecided.

But Repair Campaign elder and former St Vincent and the Grenadines prime minister Ralph Gonsalves pointed to disaggregated data showing that support was considerably higher among younger people, with 60% of those aged 18-24 and 51% of those aged 25-34 backing a meeting on reparatory justice.
The poll also suggested that a majority of all ages who voted Labour (58%) and Liberal Democrat (57%) in the last election favoured a meeting.
The findings come as the UK faces intensifying pressure from Caribbean leaders to apologise for its role in slavery and agree to a structured dialogue on reparations.

“The bulk of the young people under the age of 35 are saying we have to have that conversation. This should prompt him, like the Dutch prime minister, to give a full formal apology,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.

He also urged King Charles to apologise and help establish mechanisms for a dialogue, adding that he was disappointed with the King’s maiden speech in the Bahamas, which he described as “falling far short of what he had said before”.

Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.

A year later he described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to “deepen my own understanding of slavery’s enduring impact”, in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.
In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.

“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”
He said the leaders at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.
Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Chogm gathering, hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.
But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.

“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.
“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.

“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – a full and formal apology – and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”

Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.

She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”
Related: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit
The chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.

Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.
Charles is to travel to Guyana on Thursday where the president, Mohamed Irfaan Ali, recently called for the monarch to take the next step and offer to apologise.
The king follows the guidance of his ministers, and it is understood the government has not advised him to offer an apology or reparations, in keeping with established policy.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will join Charles in Antigua for the gathering of Commonwealth leaders.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “At the request of host governments, the king’s programme will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future that are having a transformative effect on the region, as it confronts the challenges of today.

“For his majesty, this tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past. This will therefore also be reflected in differing ways and words during the tour, as you would expect.”
Announcing the poll results, Repair Campaign founder Denis O’Brien called for a “time-lined commitment to holding talks with Caribbean states”.

“To date, there have been too many unsubstantiated expressions of regret and sorrow about Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, coupled with empty promises – including at the last Chogm in Samoa – that some sort of dialogue would begin,” he said.
Additional reporting by Press Association

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: We asked you - what do you want from the Burnham government’s first budget?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: First Edition readers and people struggling with the cost of living tell us what the government could do to improve their lives
body: Good morning. Don’t expect anything radical. This, the Treasury has been at pains to tell us, will be a very “low-key” budget. After weeks of speculation from journalists, a flurry of press releases from thinktanks, and a photoshoot with an obligatory red box, the chancellor, John Healey, will announce the details of the Burnham government’s first budget in the Commons today at 12:30pm.

Healey has been selling this as a series of measures designed to relieve pressure on low- and middle-income households under the mangled tagline of “breathing space for today, fresh hope for the future”. Many of the proposals have already been briefed, and their modesty is a sign of the constraints – both real and self-imposed – that his government faces. He has rejected calls to raise capital gains tax or lower the mansion tax and has promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules, while the Iran war has increased the cost of borrowing and eroded his spending power.

Voters might be hoping for something transformative from a government that risks presiding over the worst parliament for living standards on record. That’s the impression I got from First Edition readers and people struggling with the cost of living, who I spoke to for this morning’s newsletter about what they’d like to see from today’s budget. First, here are the headlines.

Israeli elections | Israel could be in for weeks of political haggling after exit polls and partial official results showed neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition bloc led by former general Gadi Eisenkot had won enough seats to form a government.

Energy | The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog.

Middle East | A multipronged peace deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted and for the Houthis to withdraw substantial forces inside Yemen are at the heart of Gulf states’ plans to avert what they regard as a disastrous renewal of war between Iran and the US.

UK news | A 78-year-old volunteer has claimed a Reform UK councillor accused her of “facilitating the invasion” and being akin to a Nazi collaborator during the second world war because she has helped asylum seekers learn English.

Brazil | The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

There was some detectable grumbling earlier this week over the lack of information about this budget compared with those of Rachel Reeves, and Healey has made much of the “military-style protocols” that have allegedly stopped the Treasury’s secrets from leaking out. But it seems more likely that there hasn’t been much to leak. “It’s going to be a far smaller budget than last year,” Kiran Stacey, the Guardian’s policy editor, told me on Monday. “It’s not going to be ending 40 years of neoliberalism.”

We’ve already covered some of its content: Patrick Butler and Pippa Crerar wrote yesterday on the government’s plan to abolish the detested rule that has plunged unpaid carers into debt (which the Guardian exposed last year). The government was criticised yesterday for pausing the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage, paid to people under 21, with the more generous “national living wage” for older workers, and has also announced a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living pressures facing UK households. That is expected to include support for poorer families with energy bills this winter and to pledge energy market reforms aimed at bringing down bills for all households in the longer term.

The extent of those pressures is remarkable. StepChange, the UK’s largest debt advice charity, pulled together some figures for this morning’s First Edition that show the average household arrears debt for their clients increased from £2,833 to £4,345 between 2022 and 2025. “In the late 2000s, people would primarily come to us with consumer credit debt,” a spokesperson from the charity told me. “But one in two people who come to us now have energy debt. These pressures are completely new.” ***What could the government do to address energy bills?

A number of readers told First Edition that energy bills are their major concern. Michael works for a small property company, and rents a three-bedroom bungalow in Winchester where he lives with his three children. It’s draughty, and he spends about £165 a month on electricity and gas, which will increase this winter. “I think about the cost of everything now,” he tells me. “Will I get enough money to be able to afford this? Will I have enough when the rent is due?”

Healey has been considering making the warm homes discount, a £150 annual reduction to electricity bills for people in receipt of benefits, more generous. But Michael doesn’t qualify for this, since he doesn’t receive benefits. After tax, his monthly income is between £2,500 and £3,000, and his rent is £1,800 a month, leaving him at most £300 each week (in a good month) to cover the living costs of four people. The warm homes discount is targeted at the most needy and does nothing for people further up the income spectrum who are still struggling.

“Alongside funded measures to provide immediate relief, the government needs a structural plan to reduce energy bills over the medium term,” Mathew Lawrence, the director of Common Wealth, a thinktank that has been cited as an influence on Burnham’s government, tells me. One idea would be an “energy guarantee”, a protected bloc of energy priced at pre-crisis levels (as Kiran reported earlier this month, energy officials are working up more radical changes that could be introduced after the budget). But Healey has ruled out some of the tax changes that could help fund this type of policy. “So decisions on tax have limited the government’s scope for action on bills,” Mathew says.

A persistent causes of stress for Michael is the rising cost of food. “Once something goes up in price, it never comes down again,” he says. This is well evidenced: one report from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, published in May, observed that when food prices in the UK have risen during crises such as the pandemic, they have either fallen slowly or incompletely, or have stayed the same indefinitely.

One of the proposals the government announced on Monday is the removal of import tariffs on products including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins. But the impact on household budgets will be pretty minimal; the Treasury estimates it will save £21 on the average yearly food shop. For Michael, who tries to limit his weekly food shop in Aldi to £80, this will barely make a dent.
What will the government do about housing costs?

This was another concern that cropped up among First Edition readers. Sue, from west Kent, wants the chancellor to announce more council housing. Burnham has committed Labour to the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar decade, and Healey is expected to announce a further £1bn in funding for this. He’ll also likely provide more details of the Your First Home scheme designed to help first-time buyers get on the property ladder, a new version of the Help to Buy scheme, which pushed up house prices and made property developers inordinately rich.

The impact of both of these measures will only be felt in the longer term. A more immediate solution would be linking local housing allowance, which has been frozen since 2024, to rents. The Resolution Foundation finds that more than 900,000 private rented households on universal credit face a shortfall between their rent and their housing allowance, averaging £158 a month for a family renting a two-bedroom home.
Finally, what about fuel prices?

Pat, from Aberdeen, told us that she’d like to see the government reduce fuel prices. The rising cost of petrol is penalising people who rely on their cars to get around, and the government has announced that it will be continuing the freeze on fuel duty, the tax levied on every litre of petrol or diesel, which Rishi Sunak announced in 2022.

But maintaining the freeze on fuel duty will largely help higher-income households, who drive more, while depriving the government of a revenue source. “Obviously some people on low incomes have to drive a lot. But they’re also struggling with the cost of living at large,” says Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation. “So instead of using this rather blunt instrument, it would be better to find other ways to help poorer households, particularly with more action on energy bills.”

After writing about the Serbian elections last week, I was glad to read Aleksandar Matković’s thoughtful analysis of their outcome and what weary European democracies can learn from the triumphant ‘bunch of students’. Libby
I found Zoe Williams’ column hilarious and self-knowing – on how the people who see you least may just know you best. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

Our Caribbean correspondent, Natricia Duncan, has been following calls for a full apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade from King Charles – this thorough piece sets out what’s a stake as he begins his tour of the region. Libby

Why won’t MPs tax the rich? This incredibly insightful piece by Faiza Shaheen asked politicians that exact question – and their answers provided useful insight on how to push the dial. Well worth a read. Poppy

After his Orwell prize-winning book Poverty Safari was referenced by Andy Burnham in his first speech in Scotland as Labour leader, writer and activist Darren McGarvey doesn’t pull punches in this interview with the National. Libby
Football | Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty in Fleetwood’s 5-3 shootout win against 10-man Arsenal, after the Carabao Cup fourth round tie finished 1-1.
Football | Michael Carrick has been given the chance to save his job by turning Manchester United’s results around, with the head coach remaining in place for Saturday’s visit to Chelsea.
Cricket | Australia fought back in a rollercoaster start to the deciding Test against South Africa, as hosts all out for 329.

“Healey targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’”, is the Guardian’s splash today. The Times leads on “Healey to cut energy bills by scrapping green levies”, the i Paper has “Burnham to target rising energy bills in high-stakes first Budget”, and the FT’s take is “Healey puts energy reform at centre of Budget aimed at steadying nerves”. Still on the budget, the Mail has £6 billion budget benefits bonanza”, the Mirror writes “A budget for workers”, and the Express says “Kemi: Labour is coming for your pay packets”.
Elsewhere, the Telegraph leads on “King: Slavery was a ‘great suffering’”, the Sun says “Arise Sir Harry”, and Metro has “Wife ‘victim of a sick fantasy’”.
Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win

Harry Kane is the men’s Ballon d’Or winner for 2026, the first Englishman to win the trophy in 25 years. At a lavish ceremony at the Palladium Theatre in London, Kane unexpectedly won ahead of co-favourites Lamine Yamal of Barcelona and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid. In a contest that has been critiqued for promoting individualism and celebrity in sport, Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s chief sports writer, Barney Ronay, about the symbolism of Kane’s win.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Amid the unrelenting tales of woe regarding social media’s impact on young minds, some enterprising gen-Z’s are working on fixes for their peers. As younger users become increasingly wearied by the attention-splicing, joy-sapping demands of social media, a growing number of companies are offering means to digitally detox while individuals are likewise getting creative.
Nineteen-year-old Shreya Nallamothu, for example, a computer science student at Duke University, has invented her own DIY Brick device to block selected apps.

“Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,” Nallamothu says. “Often the tech companies’ best interests aren’t in the users’ best interests. Social media has gotten away from what good technology can do, and people have noticed.”
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say
articles.summary: Far-right senator and his family boarded private plane to Ecuador after crossing border to Argentina, Argentina’s government confirms
body: The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who called the act “shameful”.

A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Argentina’s government confirmed that Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters had crossed the border into Argentina and boarded a private flight to Ecuador, at 11.30pm on Tuesday night.

“They did so with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment to entering the country,” Argentina’s National Directorate of Migration said on X. “Furthermore, the transits were recorded by the competent authority without incident.”
Related: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after Brazil election loss

The flight, the agency said, was operated by the company Baires Fly SA and bound for Guayaquil, 260km (160 miles) south-west of the Ecuadorian capital, Quito. The Bolsonaros entered Argentina via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing in the province of Misiones, it added.

Lula condemned Bolsonaro’s apparent decision to flee. “This is what the family Bolsonaro are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he’s become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.

“I keep imagining what’s on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that Bolsonaro was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of the morning.
A US state department spokesperson said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted visas “to allow them entry into the United States”.
Lawmakers from Lula’s Workers’ party asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notices list.
Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.

A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.

A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.

Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.

The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off. It is unclear if that flight was the same plane the Bolsonaros used to flee to Ecuador.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Lula, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”
One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.
The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.

As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.
The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.

Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.

The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.

Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by pushing Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.
Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.
“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.

Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.

Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.

“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.

Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was ensured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.

Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.

Speaking in Brasília, Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of his candidate’s departure. “Because yesterday we talked about the need for Flávio, with the 60m votes he received, to take on this role as leader of the opposition … since we were given a mandate by a significant part of the population,” he said.

Asked whether he believed Bolsonaro could lead the opposition from abroad, he said: “María Corina Machado did it” with her country, Venezuela.

Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.
Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.

Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.

“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.
